description: LUMEN es un sistema autónomo de soporte vital para misiones aeroespaciales. Integra precisión electromecánica y control inteligente para brindar soporte respiratorio en microgravedad y salud pública en la tierra.
summary:
LUMEN (Universal Life-Support and Medical Equipment for Space Navigation) is an autonomous life-support system and virtual respiratory therapist designed for deep-space exploration missions (Moon/Mars). 
What did you develop?
An integrated platform featuring a gravity independent harmonic cam mechanical ventilator and intelligent software. It replaces physical airflow sensors with an AI Virtual Pressure Sensor that processes motor current consumption to estimate real time airway pressure and lung resistance.
How does it address the challenge?
During a sudden medical crisis halfway to Mars where acute chest pain or collapse leads to respiratory failure, hypoxia, or severe acidosis (the 5Hs/5Ts of ACLS) with a 20 minute signal delay and no physician onboard, LUMEN acts autonomously. It monitors respiration rate (12–20 BPM, NASA-STD-3001 standard), delivers a protective tidal volume of 300–500 mL with a 1:2 I:E ratio (NASA physiological standards for CO2 clearance in microgravity), and triggers a safety cutoff (PWM 0 at 35 cmH2O) to prevent barotrauma, guiding non-medical crew via an intuitive HMI.
Why is it important?
It ensures crew survival and medical autonomy in deep space while serving as accessible dual-use healthcare technology for isolated rural communities on Earth.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?
LUMEN (Universal Life-Support and Medical Equipment for Space Navigation) is an autonomous life-support system and virtual respiratory therapist featuring an emergency mechanical ventilator driven by a harmonic cam and an intelligent biomedical monitoring platform. The harmonic cam (40 mm base radius, 76 mm maximum lift) converts DC motor rotation into smooth inspiratory compression (120° phase) and assisted expiratory return (150° phase), delivering a protective tidal volume of 300 to 500 mL with a 1:2 I:E ratio (aligned with NASA physiological standards for active CO₂ clearance in microgravity). It replaces fragile physical airflow sensors with an AI virtual pressure sensor: a model computing real time airway pressure directly from motor current consumption (ACS712 sensor). Grounded in international clinical standards of BLS (Basic Life Support), ACLS (Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support), and ATLS (Advanced Trauma Life Support), and aligned with NASA space emergency protocols (NASA FDF Medical Checklist / ExMC), it monitors respiration rate (12–20 BPM, NASA-STD-3001 standard) and triggers an immediate safety cutoff (PWM 0 at 35 cmH₂O) to prevent barotrauma during deep-space medical crises involving physical trauma, hypoxia, collapse, or respiratory acidosis halfway to Mars.

2. What benefits does it offer?

Medical autonomy during deep space delays: Enables non-physician crew members to apply AI guided BLS, ACLS, and ATLS clinical algorithms to manage respiratory acidosis, chest trauma, and acute hypoventilation crises during deep-space exploration missions (NASA DRM 8/9), where extreme distances and communication delays prevent real time Earth medical support.

Mechanical robustness in microgravity: Eliminating exposed physical airflow sensors prevents calibration drift, clogging, and mechanical failures in weightlessness.

Intuitive HMI dashboard: The system features a high-contrast, clinical-grade Human-Machine Interface (HMI) built in Python (Pygame) for rapid situational awareness during medical emergencies. Divided into two functional zones, the left panel provides an interactive power slider that maps motor drive percentage directly to respiratory rate with color-coded safety alerts for bradypnea and tachypnea. The right panel displays a real-time airway pressure oscilloscope (cmH₂O) inferred from motor current load, paired with a dynamic Virtual Respiratory Therapist (AI) diagnostic module and a prominent Total Emergency Stop button for immediate manual override.

3. What is the expected impact of the project?

Deep space exploration impact (Mars): Secures crew survival during acute medical emergencies, physical trauma, or environmental life-support (ECLSS) failures in deep space.

Terrestrial dual-use impact: Functions as an affordable, intelligent life-support technology for isolated rural clinics, disaster zones, and low-resource settings lacking intensive care specialists.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, software, and data sources did you use?

Physical hardware (TRL 3-4): High-impact treated wood chassis and 8 mm acrylic protective walls for proof-of-concept testing, standard AMBU resuscitation bag, high-torque DC motor, arduino microcontroller, ACS712 (30A) Hall current sensor, and IBT-2 (43A) H-bridge driver.

Software and Languages: C/C++ (Arduino IDE closed-loop firmware and safety interrupts) and Python.

Space agency data sources and standards: Official NASA Technical Standard NASA Health and Medical Care Section 3.0, NASA Technical Memorandum TM-2013-217377, ISS biomedical spaceflight study by Baevsky et al. (2007), biological datasets from NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), and human health standards from NASA Human Research Program (HRP).

5. How is your project creative?
In its AI Virtual Sensing Innovation: instead of adding fragile pneumatic sensors prone to failure in space, LUMEN leverages electromechanical coupling physics to convert motor current consumption (Amperes) into a non-invasive pulmonary pressure gauge, solving sensor vulnerability in spaceflight.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Medical and NASA standards: Strict compliance with NASA-STD-3001, NASA Health and Medical Care Section 3.0 (12–20 BPM, 300–500 mL tidal volume, 35 cmH₂O protective ceiling), the 5 Space Hazards from the NASA Human Research Program (HRP), and the integration of international BLS, ACLS, and ATLS protocols adapted for deep-space flight (NASA FDF Medical Checklist / ExMC).

Spaceflight material roadmap: The current low-cost wood and acrylic prototype structure is projected to migrate toward medical-grade PEEK or anodized 6061-T6 aluminum to eliminate outgassing and flammability risks in certified flight models.
